clinicalPearls: The commonest renal fusion anomaly, in which the two kidneys are joined, most often at their lower poles, by an isthmus of renal parenchyma or fibrous tissue crossing the midline
The isthmus is typically arrested beneath the inferior mesenteric artery during ascent, so the kidney sits lower than normal and its collecting systems and vessels are anomalous

Often asymptomatic and found incidentally, but there is an increased risk of ureteropelvic junction obstruction, stone formation, and infection because of high ureteric insertion and impaired drainage

Associated with an increased incidence of certain malignancies, including Wilms tumour in children and, in adults, renal and transitional cell tumours, as well as a reported association with retroperitoneal sarcoma of the isthmus
The blood supply is highly variable, often with multiple accessory arteries, which is important before any surgery
May be associated with other anomalies and syndromes, including Turner syndrome and trisomy 18
Management is directed at complications such as obstruction (pyeloplasty), stones, or tumour; the anomaly itself needs no treatment when asymptomatic
reference.pathophysiology: A horseshoe kidney forms during early development when the two metanephric masses fuse across the midline, usually at their lower poles, before normal ascent and rotation are complete. As the fused kidney ascends it is halted by the inferior mesenteric artery catching the isthmus, so the kidney remains low and incompletely rotated, with anteriorly directed pelves and high ureteric insertions. These anatomical features impair urinary drainage and predispose to ureteropelvic junction obstruction, stasis, calculus formation, and infection. The variable and often multiple vascular supply reflects the abnormal position and developmental history of the fused kidney.
additionalDifferentials: Bilateral ureteropelvic junction obstruction of normally positioned kidneys
additionalInvestigations: Renal ultrasound to identify the isthmus and hydronephrosis
CT or MR urography to define anatomy, vasculature, and any obstruction or tumour
MAG3 diuretic renogram to assess drainage and differential function
Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) if reflux is suspected
redFlags: Symptomatic ureteropelvic junction obstruction with pain or declining function
Recurrent or obstructing calculi with infection
A solid mass arising from the isthmus or a renal moiety suggesting malignancy
reference.prognosis: Most horseshoe kidneys are asymptomatic and compatible with normal life expectancy; prognosis worsens only when complications such as obstruction, recurrent stones, infection, or tumour arise, and these are generally manageable with targeted treatment.
pitfalls: Failing to map the anomalous and often multiple vessels before surgery on the isthmus or a renal unit
Missing an isthmic tumour by not imaging the parenchyma crossing the midline
Attributing all flank pain to the anomaly and overlooking a treatable obstruction or stone
Overlooking associated syndromic conditions in children
management: Manage asymptomatic incidental cases conservatively with reassurance and periodic surveillance
Relieve ureteropelvic junction obstruction surgically with pyeloplasty when symptomatic or causing deteriorating drainage or function
Treat calculi with appropriate lithotripsy, ureteroscopy or percutaneous techniques, allowing for the abnormal anatomy and impaired drainage
Treat urinary tract infections promptly with culture-directed antibiotics and address predisposing stasis and reflux
Define the variable, often multiple arterial supply with CT or MR angiography before any surgery
Maintain surveillance for the increased tumour risk, including Wilms tumour in children and renal and transitional cell tumours in adults
Refer to urology and screen for associated anomalies and syndromes such as Turner syndrome and trisomy 18
